prize_parts.citation: For the detection of the baryon acoustic peak in the large-scale distribution of galaxies, establishing a standard ruler for measuring the expansion history of the universe

statement.case_for: Baryon acoustic oscillations are exactly what I mean by a clue from nature. A sound-wave imprint from the early plasma, a feature at roughly 150 Mpc, was found independently and simultaneously in SDSS and 2dFGRS in 2005. It has since been recovered by 6dFGS, WiggleZ, BOSS, eBOSS and DESI. It turns the dark-energy question from an inference into a measured expansion history, with systematics that are unusually well controlled because the ruler is set by simple linear physics. Its importance is growing: the present debate over whether dark energy evolves rests largely on BAO distances. The attribution is as clean as large surveys allow, since two teams reached the same discovery at the same time, and Eisenstein, Cole and Peacock represent both.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is that this is a measurement within a programme already honoured three times (2006 CMB, 2011 accelerating expansion, 2019 cosmology), so the committee may see it as repetition. It is also survey-collaboration science, and the theory of the acoustic peak (Peebles and Yu, Sunyaev and Zeldovich) lies outside the credited names, so a three-person trio is partly artificial. Finally, only two colleagues put it in their top five, so my first place reflects my own weighting more than a committee view. The optical lattice clock has far wider opening support, and I cannot dismiss that.

responses.point: Optical lattice clocks are a measurement technique in the purest sense, now reaching 1e-18 uncertainty, enabling relativistic geodesy and a coming redefinition of the second, and the credit to Katori and Ye is a clean pair.
responses.response: I agree that the credit is clean and that the maturity is beyond doubt. My reservation is the one I raised in my own ballot: is this a discovery or a superb instrument? You argue its value is the limit of what can be measured. That is fair, but the case for a physics prize is stronger when the clock yields clues from nature, such as drift of constants or a dark-matter signal, and so far these are limits, not detections. I accept it as a serious candidate and would not block it, but I do not think the precision argument by itself makes it first. The second's redefinition belongs to metrology, not to the prize criterion.

responses.point: Topological insulators are the discovery he most looks for: a clear physical idea, quantitative theory and experiments that confirm it, with a very large influence on condensed-matter physics, in a Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio.
responses.response: The physics is deep and I rank it second myself. My difficulty is attribution rather than merit. You note yourself that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang (the HgTe prediction that Molenkamp's experiment tested), Moore, Balents and Hasan are left out, and the 2016 prize already covered topological phases. A trio that omits the author of the very proposal Molenkamp confirmed will be criticised. If colleagues can show a defensible three-name definition, I will move it up, but today I think the credit problem is more severe than for BAO.

responses.point: IceCube opened a new observational window with the diffuse astrophysical neutrino flux and the first sources, TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068 and the Galactic plane, with Halzen and Karle as the decisive leaders.
responses.response: This is the candidate closest to my own taste for a discovery from nature, and I rank it fourth. I would still qualify two points. The source population for most of the flux remains unresolved, so the astrophysical meaning is less settled than your maturity assessment suggests. And a two-name credit for a collaboration of hundreds, with AMANDA and DUMAND history behind it, needs more scrutiny than for BAO, where two independent teams reached the same result. I want expert reports on the IceCube credit before I support it as the lead.

responses.point: Circuit QED gives a conceptually clean extension of cavity QED onto a chip, underpins essentially all superconducting processors, and is a distinct discovery from the work recognised in 2025.
responses.response: The 2004 strong-coupling result is real and well established. But I am uneasy about it for two reasons. The 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits makes a second prize in the same area so soon hard to justify, and much of the weight here comes from quantum-computing architecture, not a new phenomenon of nature. I also note that Girvin and Devoret are outside the credited names. I put it below the clock, and I do not think it is first-rank.

uncertainties: Whether the committee wants the BAO measurement itself or would require the wider programme of survey cosmology, and whether a trio of Eisenstein, Cole and Peacock can be defended against the Peebles and Sunyaev-Zeldovich theoretical roots.
Whether a third cosmology prize in two decades would be seen as a repeat, given earlier awards in 2006, 2011 and 2019.

Whether optical lattice clocks should be treated as a discovery of nature or as a precision instrument, and how much weight the committee gives to still-pending tests of constants and the redefinition of the second.
Whether recent DESI results on evolving dark energy will firm up soon enough to strengthen the cosmology case or complicate it.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for any shortlisted candidate. My research on dark energy and de Sitter space is in the same broad area as BAO, which affects my scientific interest but not any personal or institutional tie to the credited names. David Gross, my PhD supervisor, is not among the candidates.
